explain.title: What is a floating-point number?
explain.body: In computers, real values, also known as floating-point numbers, are used to represent number with fractions and/or decimals. A floating-point number = sign × mantissa × 2^exponent.

explain.title: Convert a decimal fraction to binary
explain.body: To convert the fractional part of a real (floating-point) number from decimal (base-10) to binary (base-2), multiply the fractional part by 2 and write down the integral part of the result. Repeat this process with the new fractional part until the value of the fractional part becomes zero or until the required precision is achieved.

explain.title: Single precision
explain.body: In this standard, 4 bytes (or 32 bits) are assigned where the 1st bit is the sign bit, and the next 8 bits are for the exponent and the remaining 23 bits are for the mantissa. The approximate range of values from 1.4 × 10⁻⁴⁵ to 3.4 × 10³⁸.

explain.title: Double precision and accuracy
explain.body: In double precision, the exponent is represented using 11 bits. The exponent is stored in a biased form, with a bias of 1023. Floating-point computations may also have round-off errors, so scientific computing requires monitoring these errors to maintain accuracy.

mistakes: Writing the integer parts in reverse order when converting a fraction to binary; record them from top to bottom.
Stopping before the fractional part reaches zero when the conversion is exact.
Confusing the exponent bits with the mantissa bits in single precision: the allocation is 1, 8, and 23 bits.
Forgetting that the exponent is stored with a bias, or stating the bias for double precision when asked about single precision.
Ignoring possible round-off errors when explaining the limits of floating-point values.
